questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, is in ED, sitting upright and very breathless, with a raised JVP and leg oedema. You tell the examiner you will examine both lung bases to tell pulmonary oedema apart from pleural effusion. Which group of findings at a base points to a pleural effusion?
options: Hyperresonant percussion with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance
Fine end-inspiratory crackles that do not clear with coughing, normal percussion
Stony dull percussion with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance
Dull percussion with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance
questions.why: Fluid in the pleural space gives stony dullness, and it muffles breath sounds and vocal resonance. Oedema in the lung tissue gives fine crackles instead, and in heart failure the two often occur together.
notes: Hyperresonance with reduced breath sounds suggests pneumothorax, not fluid.
Fine crackles that persist after coughing are the sign of interstitial or alveolar oedema in the lung tissue, not fluid in the pleural space.
Dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance means consolidation, where solid lung carries sound better.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, has acute pulmonary oedema in ED. He has smoked about 30 pack-years and uses tiotropium. On room air his SpO2 is 87%. His venous gas shows pH 7.31 and pCO2 56 mmHg with a normal bicarbonate. The nurse is putting oxygen back on and asks what saturation to aim for. What is the most appropriate SpO2 target?
options: 88 to 92%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
92 to 96%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
94 to 98%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
98 to 100%, using a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
questions.why: TSANZ guidance sets a target of 88 to 92% for anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. A smoker on tiotropium with acute respiratory acidosis (raised pCO2, low pH) qualifies. Too much oxygen can worsen his CO2 retention, so confirm with an arterial gas.
notes: 92 to 96% is the TSANZ target for most acutely ill adults, but he is at risk of hypercapnia, which calls for a lower target.
94 to 98% is the older UK target for patients without hypercapnic risk, and it is too high for a patient who is already retaining CO2.
Aiming for near-100% saturation causes hyperoxia, which can worsen hypercapnia and acidosis in a patient at risk of CO2 retention.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, has hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema with BP 184/100. After a further sublingual dose of glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) and the start of an IV GTN infusion, he breathes more easily within minutes and his BP falls to 170/92. What is the main mechanism of this early benefit?
options: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing natriuresis
Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing contractility and stroke volume
Blockade of arteriolar L-type calcium channels, causing marked afterload reduction
Nitric oxide release raising cGMP in venous smooth muscle, venodilating to reduce preload
questions.why: Nitrates release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle. At low doses this mainly dilates veins, which lowers venous return and LV filling pressure. Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure falls and less fluid leaks into the lung tissue. Higher doses also dilate arterioles and reduce afterload.
notes: This is how furosemide works. Its diuretic effect takes longer, and GTN does not act on the kidney.
Nitrates are not inotropes; beta-1 agonists such as dobutamine are kept for cardiogenic shock.

Nitrates do reduce afterload at higher doses, but through nitric oxide and cGMP, not calcium channel blockade. The calcium channel blocker verapamil is negatively inotropic and should be avoided in acute heart failure.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, had an MI 12 years ago and coronary bypass surgery 10 years ago. Today's ECG shows sinus tachycardia with pathological Q waves, poor R wave progression and T wave inversion in V1 to V3, unchanged from an ECG 2 years ago. Which coronary artery was most likely occluded in his previous infarct?
options: Right coronary artery, proximal to its acute marginal branch
questions.why: V1 to V4 look at the interventricular septum and the anterior wall, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. An old anteroseptal infarct with poor R wave progression fits an LAD occlusion. Loss of anterior myocardium is a common cause of ischaemic cardiomyopathy.
notes: An RCA occlusion usually causes an inferior infarct (II, III, aVF), sometimes with right ventricular or posterior involvement, not Q waves in V1 to V3.
A circumflex occlusion usually affects the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) or the posterior wall, not V1 to V3.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum, which show up in the inferior leads, not as anteroseptal Q waves.
